metadata.title: What kind of individual support activities in interventions foster pre-service and beginning teachers’ self-efficacy? A meta-analysis

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This paper is a systematic review and meta-analysis of (quasi-)experimental intervention studies on teacher self-efficacy, not an analysis of ILSA microdata (e.g., PISA/TALIS student records). Therefore, there is no student-level sampling frame, no plausible-value (PV) scaling, and no ILSA complex survey design to which sampling or replicate weights would apply. The quantitative synthesis uses random-effects meta-analytic aggregation with robust variance estimation (RVE) to account for dependency among multiple effect sizes per primary study, rather than survey weighting. As a result, the concept of “weights” here refers to meta-analytic variance handling across studies/effects, not to population-representative survey weights.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PVs) are not applicable because the study does not analyze ILSA achievement scales with PVs; instead, it synthesizes effect sizes (Hedges’ g) from primary intervention studies measuring teacher self-efficacy. The paper also does not report an imputation or deletion strategy for missing data at the microdata level because it does not use a single pooled dataset of student responses. Missing-data handling is therefore not part of the methodological pipeline in the way it would be for an empirical ILSA microdata analysis.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The meta-analysis included quantitative intervention studies targeting pre-service teachers (PSTs) or beginning teachers (BTs) in their first year of teaching, with teacher self-efficacy as the dependent variable. Studies were included if they used (quasi-)experimental pre-posttest control-group designs, pre-posttest designs without control groups, or posttest designs with control groups. Exclusions were applied for studies focusing only on special-needs/sports/low-income teaching contexts (to avoid strong content deviation) and for studies lacking sufficient quantitative statistics (e.g., missing means/SDs per group) to compute effect sizes. After screening, the authors removed three studies with small group sizes (n ≤ 10 per experimental group) and further removed four outlier effects based on standardized deleted residuals (SDRs) with thresholds below −1.96 or above 1.96, yielding a final set of 28 studies and 49 effect sizes.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2009 the study leveraged the reported predictors to predict Literature synthesis outcome (not student-level prediction), finding that This article is a systematic review and meta-analysis (not an ILSA microdata study) synthesizing 28 intervention studies (49 effects) on how individual support activities in mentoring/coaching/supervision/program interventions affect teacher self-efficacy for pre-service teachers (PSTs) and beginning teachers (BTs). The authors computed Hedges’ g for each effect size (using pooled pretest SDs for designs without control groups; using reported means/SDs or ANOVA statistics for control-group designs) and then estimated an overall random-effects model with robust variance estimation (RVE) to handle multiple dependent effects per study. The overall intervention effect was medium and statistically significant: Hedges’ g = 0.678 (SE = 0.064, p < .001, CI [0.547, 0.809], I2 = 90.133). In moderator analyses, providing feedback on lesson plans showed the largest effect size (Model 1: g = 1.033, SE = 0.273, p = .056; Model 2: g = 0.849, SE = 0.785, p = .082), though it did not reach conventional significance after additional controls. Limitations include reliance on study-level coding of intervention components, small numbers for some moderators, and no country-level moderator testing despite cross-country inclusion. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to ILSA-specific fields because the paper does not use ILSA microdata (e.g., TALIS/PISA student records) and does not train or evaluate machine-learning models. Instead, it performs a meta-analytic synthesis of effect sizes from primary (quasi-)experimental intervention studies, so PV handling, missing-data imputation/deletion at the microdata level, and ML algorithm fields are not applicable. The country list is derived from the included primary studies’ locations, but per-country student Ns are not reported in the provided text.
